author: Rohit Phaniram Sakamuri
title: Valid but Blind: Tent's Entropy Step Reduces the Sensitivity of a Label-Free Risk Monitor, and an Entropy-Free Twin Recovers Much of It

blocks.text: Abstract

Test-time adaptation allows an image classifier to update itself on incoming images without using their labels. However, the model also needs a way to detect when its performance becomes poor. This project studies a confidence-based risk monitor and asks whether adaptation can make its warnings less useful. Experiments used CIFAR-100-C, six published model checkpoints, and streams with strongly unequal class frequencies. Under Tent adaptation, the monitor missed 147 of 166 clear risk violations, compared with 44 of 110 for frozen models. Further comparisons showed that Tent's entropy update added missed warnings beyond changes in batch-normalization statistics alone. A second copy of the classifier, called an entropy-free twin, reduced missed violations on held-out corruption families to 30 of 115, with five false alarms in 121 safe streams. The working twin provides a useful warning signal in this setting, but does not provide a certified bound on error.
Motivation

A classifier trained on clear images may later receive blurred, noisy, or poorly lit images. Its training data may also contain a different balance of classes. For example, a deployed camera might see many more vehicles than animals, even though both were common during training. These changes can affect classification accuracy.

Updating the model on incoming images can help, but adaptation can also make incorrect predictions more confident. In deployment, the correct labels may arrive late or never arrive at all. It is therefore difficult to check accuracy directly.

The difficulty becomes more serious when the warning system reads the same confidence scores that adaptation changes. The classifier may become more certain without becoming more accurate, leaving fewer warning signals for the monitor. This project examines that interaction and tests whether a second copy of the model, without entropy updates, can provide a more useful alarm.
Literature Review
Test-time adaptation and normalization

Wang et al. introduced Tent, which adapts a model by reducing the entropy of its predictions [1]. Entropy measures how spread out the predicted class probabilities are. Reducing it encourages definite predictions, but does not directly check whether those predictions are correct. Tent updates normalization parameters using unlabeled test data. Schneider et al. studied adaptation through batch-normalization statistics [3]. Their approach is an important control because it allows the model to respond to a changed input distribution without Tent's entropy gradient step.
Monitoring without target labels

Schirmer et al. proposed a sequential risk monitor for test-time adaptation [2]. The monitor uses uncertainty as a substitute for unavailable labels and raises an alarm when a lower bound on error exceeds a tolerated level. Their paper also reports cases where the uncertainty proxy becomes too loose to detect poor performance. A valid lower bound can therefore be unhelpful: saying that error is at least 3% tells us little if the actual error is 50%.
Confidence, accuracy and class skew

AETTA, by Lee et al., studies accuracy estimation during adaptation and reports that Tent's confidence can rise while accuracy falls [4]. Amin and Kim also analyze over-certainty in adaptation algorithms [10]. Cygert et al. show difficulties with unsupervised model selection on corrupted data with unequal class frequencies [6]. These findings motivate evaluating missed alarms under class skew, rather than assuming that results on balanced corruption data will carry over.
Stable adaptation and separate monitoring signals

SAR aims to stabilize adaptation through sample filtering and sharpness-aware optimization [5]. It provides a useful comparison with Tent. Han et al. describe adaptation masking the signal used by its own monitor in a forecasting setting and study a frozen reference model [11]. Separate monitoring signals are therefore an established idea. This project's contribution is the specific adapted-versus-frozen alarm comparison, the controls separating normalization from entropy updates, and an empirical evaluation of a twin alarm. It does not claim to discover confidence failure for the first time.
Problem Statement

Can test-time adaptation reduce a label-free risk monitor's ability to detect poor classification performance? The specific concern is that Tent changes the model's predicted probabilities, while the monitor uses those probabilities to identify uncertain predictions. The monitor may then receive fewer warning signals even when many predictions remain incorrect.

The project examines this on corrupted and class-skewed image streams. It compares Tent with a frozen classifier, separates the effects of threshold recalibration and normalization, and tests whether a second model without entropy updates can recover detection sensitivity. The issue is missed warnings, rather than a contradiction of the monitor's statistical guarantee.
Objectives
Compare missed warnings for Tent-adapted and frozen classifiers on the same stream draws.
Separate threshold recalibration, batch-normalization updates and entropy minimization.
Check whether the monitoring gap also appears with SAR.
Develop an entropy-free twin alarm and select its rule on development corruptions.
Evaluate missed violations and false alarms separately, including a test of adaptation-caused failures.
Data Collection Details

The study used the public CIFAR-100-C benchmark, based on CIFAR-100 images with common corruptions [7]. The task is to classify each image into one of 100 classes. No new photographs or manual annotations were collected. The experiments used released model weights from RobustBench [8], rather than training new classifiers from scratch.

blocks.text: Dirichlet sampling creates unequal class frequencies. With the value 0.1 used here, a few classes can dominate a stream. Images were sampled with replacement, so 12,000 observations do not mean 12,000 different images. All compared arms within a study received the same stream draws.

Target labels were used to construct the class-skewed streams and to score results afterwards. Adaptation and online alarm decisions did not receive them. The monitor did use labeled clean calibration data to select its uncertainty threshold. Thus, label-free refers to target-time operation, not the complete absence of labels from the project.

The main replication covered 504 streams. The factorial comparison covered 768 streams, and the authors' pipeline check covered 112. Further runs evaluated SAR and the twin alarm. These are related stream trials that reuse models, image pools and corruption types, rather than independent datasets. Rules were recorded before each run, but the selected models and some evaluation image IDs had already been used in earlier project work. The later runs should not be described as a completely untouched final test.

The experiments used PyTorch on RTX 4090 GPUs, with SAR, twin and adaptation-harm runs on an H100. Python environments and execution were managed with uv. The separate adaptation-harm test used clean images and severity-1 corruptions with deliberately larger Tent learning rates.
ML Models

Six pretrained image-classification checkpoints were used. They are convolutional neural networks, including residual and wide residual architectures. Their image-processing layers were already trained before this study. AugMix models use a training method designed to improve robustness through mixed image augmentations [9]. The study compares adaptation and monitoring on these checkpoints; it does not compare newly trained architectures.

blocks.text: Adaptation methods
The released checkpoint remains fixed. It provides the baseline for both classification error and monitor sensitivity.
The model uses statistics from the current test batch without a gradient update. This measures what normalization changes alone contribute.
Tent updates batch-normalization parameters by minimizing prediction entropy [1]. The main setting used Adam with a learning rate of 0.001. A lower-rate comparison used 0.0001.

SAR filters unreliable samples and uses sharpness-aware optimization [5]. The extension used its default learning rate of 0.00025. A departure from its published setup was the use of the study's BN-based models with all BN layers updated. Its results therefore refer to this implementation setting.
Risk monitor and twin alarm

The released monitor flags a prediction when its uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Uncertainty is one minus the largest predicted class probability. The threshold is chosen to maximize F1 on the clean calibration set and is recalibrated after each adaptation step. A confidence sequence, which allows repeated checks as data arrive [12], supplies a running lower bound. The monitor alarms when the bound exceeds clean source error by 0.10.

The twin is a second copy of the same checkpoint. It uses test-batch normalization but takes no entropy gradient steps. The selected rule flags an image if the twin is uncertain or the two classifiers predict different classes. This rule was chosen on noise and blur corruptions and then evaluated on weather and digital corruptions. The twin is not a fully frozen source model, because its normalization statistics respond to each batch. The working rule is a detector without a certified error bound.
Performance Analysis
Evaluation measures

Classification error is the fraction of predictions that are wrong. Let r0 be error on the clean calibration images. A strict violation is a stream with mean error at least r0 + 0.15 and last-quarter error below 0.85. The latter condition excludes extreme collapse from the main comparison. The alarm level is lower, at r0 + 0.10, so the violation has a margin above the tolerated level.

The missed-violation rate is the number of strict violations receiving no alarm divided by the total strict violations. Lower is better. The false-alarm rate is the proportion of safe streams that raise an alarm; safe streams have mean error below r0 + 0.10 without collapse. Each arm is scored on its own qualifying violations, so denominators can differ even when the stream draws are shared.
Main replication

blocks.caption: Table 3. Missed violations in the replication

blocks.text: Tent's missed share was higher in all six checkpoints. The monitor authors' own pipeline reproduced the pattern: 40/40 Tent violations were missed, compared with 10/28 for the frozen source. This check required a disclosed CIFAR-100 calibration-loader patch and replacement of the input stream at runtime. Alarm decisions matched the project's implementation on 99.1% of the 112 streams.
Separating normalization and entropy updates

blocks.caption: Table 4. Factorial comparison and SAR extension

blocks.text: Fixing Tent's threshold did not remove the gap. Recalibration recovered some sensitivity, but Tent still missed more violations than normalization alone in every checkpoint. Normalization alone did not produce a consistent gap over the frozen source, although its performance varied across models. SAR was evaluated in an additional run using the factorial study's comparison arms. Its frozen extension rule was not met. SAR selected only 4-9% of samples on four models, so this does not establish that SAR solves the problem.

An exploratory breakdown helps explain the result. Average error was similar for source and Tent, about 0.53 and 0.51, while the share of errors flagged fell from about 86% to 57%. The share of flagged predictions that were wrong remained close to 70%. In other words, many errors became invisible to the uncertainty flag. This breakdown was performed after the main verdicts and is explanatory analysis, rather than a separately confirmed mechanism.
Twin-alarm results

blocks.caption: Table 5. Missed violations on held-out corruption families

blocks.text: The selected twin reduced the missed share in all six models and met its frozen held-out rule. These violations were shared by Tent and the twin; they did not establish detection of harm unique to adaptation. The twin alarm raised five false alarms in 121 safe streams, or 4.1%, including balanced and clean controls. On the same safe skewed streams, the twin raised 3/46 false alarms and the released monitor 2/46. The larger safe-stream set should not be confused with a directly matched comparison of false-alarm rates.

The certified twin forms missed every strict violation. The useful result therefore belongs to the uncertified detector. It also remained weak on the three Addepalli models, where it missed 29/46 violations. These results show an improvement in the evaluated setting, rather than reliable detection for every checkpoint.

A separate test deliberately increased Tent's learning rate to cause failures while the twin remained below the alarm level. The twin detected 51/61 target failures, compared with 23/61 for the released monitor. However, 56 of the 61 targets were extreme collapses. One of only six safe streams also alarmed, so the combined frozen detection-and-false-alarm rule was not met. The safe sample was too small to establish the false-alarm rate in this regime.
Result and Conclusion

The study found that a statistically valid risk monitor can still have poor detection sensitivity. Under strong class skew and corruption, Tent produced substantially more missed warnings than the frozen source model. Fixed-threshold and normalization-only controls showed that the entropy step added to this gap. The same gap was not established for SAR at its tested settings.

An entropy-free twin recovered much of the lost sensitivity on the evaluated corruption families. Its working form is a practical warning rule, not a certified risk estimate. It detected many extreme adaptation-caused collapses, but the evidence for subtler harm and false alarms in that separate regime remains limited.

The experiments cover one dataset and one strong class-skew construction, with repeated images and related stream trials. Some evaluation image IDs had been used earlier. The twin has not been compared against all existing monitoring alternatives, and no general novelty claim is established. The next useful steps are other datasets, comparisons at matched false-alarm rates, and a new adaptation-harm test with enough safe and non-collapsed streams set in advance.
